item.title: BNP tightens discipline, moves to strengthen organisation
item.description:
The BNP has adopted a tougher organisational approach to enforcing party discipline and strengthening its structure, with recent actions targeting allegations of misconduct and irregularities. At the same time, efforts are underway to revitalise key units in Dhaka and expand activities at the grassroots level.
In recent weeks, the party has signalled a zero-tolerance stance through the expulsion of leaders and activists, the dissolution of committees and an order for a lawmaker to resign. It has also begun reorganising key organisational units in Dhaka, expanding grassroots activities and prioritising clean reputations, organisational experience and public engagement in leadership selection.
BNP Standing Committee member Selima Rahman said the party had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards wrongdoing.
“We have a zero-tolerance policy against any wrongdoing. The prime minister is also taking a strict stance, and I think this is the right policy,” she said.
She said BNP leaders and activists had faced repression and persecution for a long time, and some may have developed an attitude after the change of power that “the Awami League did it, so I will do it too”.
“Such behaviour is not acceptable,” she said.
“Party discipline will be maintained at any cost. At the same time, when allegations are raised, they are being verified and organisational action is being taken accordingly,” Selima Rahman said.
The central leadership's position has also been reflected in several recent incidents.
Reserved women's seat lawmaker Ferdousi Ahmed Misty was instructed by the prime minister to resign following allegations of an attack, vandalism and looting at the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur. She has denied the allegations and called for an investigation to clarify the matter.
Earlier, three key organisational committees in Dhaka were dissolved, including the 51-member convening committee of Dhaka North BNP, Dhaka North Jubo Dal and Dhaka West Chhatra Dal.
During the same period, 14 leaders and activists of the BNP and its affiliated and associate organisations were expelled over allegations of violating party discipline and engaging in unethical activities deemed unacceptable by the party.
However, not all the committee dissolutions were directly linked to the Radda centre incident, and the relevant notices did not mention the incident.
No specific reason was given for dissolving the Dhaka North BNP committee, although the party said a new committee would be formed. Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal, meanwhile, said their respective committees had been dissolved because their terms had expired.
Party sources said the central leadership had issued strict warnings against using the BNP's identity for personal gain.
District and metropolitan leaders have been instructed to monitor the activities of party leaders and activists in their respective areas and promptly inform the central leadership if anyone is found using the party's identity to exert influence, engaging in extortion, occupying property, seeking personal benefits or taking the law into their own hands.
BNP leaders said keeping the party organisation active had become increasingly important alongside running the government.
Having returned to power after a long period in opposition, the central leadership has stepped up scrutiny of grassroots leaders and activists, as well as the effectiveness of local organisational units.
Sources said a joint meeting held at the BNP's central office in September decided to increase political and organisational activities across the country.
Local units were instructed to keep party offices active, hold regular organisational meetings and programmes, strengthen communication among leaders at the thana and ward levels, and maintain a visible organisational presence in their respective areas.
The meeting also instructed party leaders to inform law enforcement agencies if they noticed suspicious activities or attempts to create disorder.
The BNP has also begun the process of selecting new leadership for Dhaka North and Dhaka South, with public acceptability and the ability to maintain effective communication with leaders and activists at the ward and thana levels among the key considerations.
The focus on the Dhaka organisation stems not only from the capital's central role in political programmes but also from the upcoming local government elections.
The north and south metropolitan units are key structures for coordinating party organisations at the ward and thana levels. Ahead of the elections, the party needs to keep its grassroots network active around potential mayoral and councillor candidates.
According to party sources, a clean image alone will not be sufficient for the new leadership. Long-standing political and organisational experience, standing by the party during difficult times, maintaining communication with grassroots leaders and activists, and the ability to mobilise the organisation when necessary are also being considered.
Discussions are therefore underway on forming the new leadership by combining experienced organisers with relatively younger leaders.
At the same time, the BNP is emphasising the need to reduce internal divisions at the grassroots level.
Party Chairman Tarique Rahman has previously stressed the importance of reaching a consensus on fielding a single candidate in each area ahead of the local government elections. Maintaining organisational unity at the ward, thana and local levels has therefore become an important consideration for the central leadership.
However, discussions are also underway on ensuring that efforts to enforce organisational discipline do not alienate leaders and activists who have remained active on the ground for years.
A senior BNP leader said: “There is no alternative to leaders with clean images if we want to restore the party's organisational tradition, strengthen Dhaka-centric politics, prepare for the upcoming local government elections and maintain political stability.”

item.title: How many more humiliations before BFF wakes up?
item.description:
Bangladesh returned from the FIFA Asean Cup having lost all three matches, conceded 13 goals and scored only two, but the numbers tell only part of the story.
The 9-2 capitulation against hosts Indonesia in Jakarta, with six goals conceded before half-time and three more in the closing minutes, has exposed deeper questions over coaching, tactical preparation, the integration of overseas-based players and, above all, the development structure of Bangladeshi football.
For a national side that arrived at the tournament with several overseas-based players, including Premier League-experienced Hamza Choudhury, the campaign ended without a point: a 3-0 defeat to Malaysia, a 1-0 loss to Singapore and finally the 9-2 rout by Indonesia.
The Indonesia result was particularly stark.
Bangladesh had not conceded nine goals in a match since the 1980s, while the nine goals equalled the most the national team has ever conceded in an international match.
The previous 9-0 defeats came against South Korea in 1979 and Iran in 1982.
The scale of the collapse has now turned what was supposed to be valuable preparation for November’s Saff Championship into a test for the Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF): whether it treats Jakarta as an isolated disaster or as evidence of problems extending far beyond one match.
Bangladesh’s problems against Indonesia were evident long before the final whistle.
Mitchell Baker struck in the 11th and 20th minutes. Indonesia added a third in the 32nd before Shahriar Emon briefly reduced the deficit four minutes later.
Baker responded almost immediately, completing his hat-trick in the 37th minute and adding another in the 42nd.
Justin Hubner then made it 6-1 in first-half stoppage time.
Bangladesh managed to stem the flow for much of the second half, but collapsed again at the end.
Luke Vickery scored in the 90th minute. Farhaan Ali Wahid pulled one back for Bangladesh in stoppage time, before Kevin Diks and Baker scored twice more, with Baker completing a five-goal haul.
The manner of the defeat has brought coach Thomas Dooley’s tactical approach under intense scrutiny.
Bangladesh struggled to deal with Indonesia’s attacks from wide areas and appeared unable to establish an effective defensive block in midfield.
There was little evidence of an adjustment capable of containing Baker even after the forward had scored twice in the opening 20 minutes.
Dooley’s decision to maintain an open approach against a technically superior and faster Indonesian side proved particularly costly as the defence was repeatedly exposed.
Shamit Shome’s injury in the 27th minute further weakened Bangladesh in midfield, but the problems continued across the pitch.
Questions have also emerged over the understanding between locally developed footballers and the growing contingent of overseas-based players.
Former Bangladesh national team coach Oscar Bruzon believes the result cannot be explained by one disastrous performance.
“To me, this 9-2 defeat against Indonesia is not merely the result of a bad match; it is the consequence of years of stagnation in Bangladeshi football,” Bruzon told Dhaka Tribune.
Bruzon, who coached Bangladesh at the 2021 Saff Championship, pointed to the national side’s performance five years ago despite limited preparation.
“We managed to secure five points from four matches. We beat Sri Lanka, drew with India and Nepal, lost to the Maldives solely due to fatigue, and remained in contention for the final until the very last match,” he said.
Five years later, Bruzon said he saw little evidence of substantial progress.
“Five years later, I find it difficult to see any clear progress, whether in the quality of the national team or, more importantly, in the underlying development structure.
“My biggest concern is how the quality of local footballers has been consistently undervalued. Bangladesh is failing to build a stable national team!”
The criticism goes to the heart of the debate now confronting the BFF: whether recruiting more overseas-based footballers can significantly improve the national side without a stronger domestic development structure beneath it.
For former national team star Ashraf Uddin Chunnu, Thursday’s defeat carried particular significance.
Forty-one years ago, he scored the winning goal when Bangladesh beat Indonesia 2-1 in a World Cup qualifying match at the National Stadium.
Watching Indonesia put nine past Bangladesh four decades later left him stunned.
“Forty-one years ago, I scored the winning goal against Indonesia in a World Cup preliminary match at the National Stadium. We won 2-1 back then,” Chunnu said.
“Yet today, I witnessed the team in such a shambolic state. Watching the game left me truly ashamed.”
Former striker Syed Rumman Bin Wali Sabbir believes the problems run considerably deeper than the senior national team.
“The core issues plaguing Bangladeshi football are structural weaknesses and a lack of planning,” he said.
“The foundation for player development has eroded due to the absence of regular leagues and competitions across the country. There is also uncertainty regarding league schedules, calendars and management.”
He also questioned how overseas-based players were being recruited.
“When selecting expatriate players, factors such as their skills, qualifications, the quality of leagues they play in and their actual performance are not being properly vetted,” Sabbir said.
“Consequently, instead of strengthening the national team, the problems persist.”
Former national team striker Jahid Hasan Ameli placed greater responsibility on Dooley and his tactical decisions.
“It was a mistake to engage in open play against Indonesia right from the start,” Ameli said.
“It was not clearly evident whether the coach had any specific plan for this match. The players, too, failed to properly discharge their responsibilities.”
The criticism is likely to intensify ahead of the Saff Championship, particularly because the Asean Cup was viewed as an opportunity to expose Bangladesh to stronger regional opposition before the home tournament.
Indonesia were undoubtedly superior opposition. They entered the match needing a large victory to beat Malaysia to the top of Group A and eventually secured their place in the final after scoring three late goals.
But the gulf in quality alone does not explain away Bangladesh’s campaign.
Three matches produced three defeats, no points, 13 goals conceded and only two scored.
Attention has therefore shifted from the players and coach to the federation responsible for the national-team program and the wider football structure.
BFF President Tabith Awal is also chairman of the federation’s National Teams Committee, according to the BFF’s current committee listing.
Awal said the federation was gathering information about what went wrong in the Asean Cup.
“We are gathering the necessary information. Important decisions will be taken at the next meeting of the National Team Committee,” he said.
Asked specifically about improving coordination between locally developed and overseas-based players and preventing a repeat of the Asean Cup failure, Awal said the issue would be discussed jointly by the National Teams Committee and Technical Committee.
“We are collecting the necessary information. Important decisions will be made during a joint meeting of the National Team Committee and the Technical Committee. I hope we will be able to achieve something positive.”
What those decisions amount to could determine whether the 9-2 defeat becomes merely another painful scoreline in Bangladesh football history or prompts a broader examination of the system that produced it.
For Bangladesh, Jakarta exposed more than a defence incapable of stopping Indonesia.
It exposed a national team still searching for a coherent structure behind it.

item.title: Sheikh Nur Islam disputes TOS Bond ownership, rejects ‘Salman’s father-in-law’ label
item.description:
Businessman Sheikh Nur Islam has denied owning the recently sealed TOS Bond Private Limited and objected to being described as “Salman’s father-in-law” in news coverage of content creator Salman Muqtadir’s activities.
However, the Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) says Sheikh Nur Islam owns the warehouse. On Saturday afternoon, Md Mehedi Hasan, Assistant Director of the DNC’s Dhaka Metro (North) office, confirmed to Dhaka Tribune that the TOS Bond warehouse is owned by Sheikh Nur Islam.
The written protest and clarification was sent on Saturday on his behalf, signed by Mohammad Foyzul Karim, Head of Operations at Fu-Wang Bowling and Services Limited.
The letter says Sheikh Nur Islam and his family never accepted the marriage of his daughter Disha Islam to Salman Muqtadir, and that all social and family ties with those concerned have been completely severed since the marriage.
In this situation, the letter calls it “undesirable, untrue and highly indecent” to link Sheikh Nur Islam’s name to Salman Muqtadir’s personal, social, business or other activities by presenting him as “Salman’s father-in-law” in news reports, headlines, videos, thumbnails or social media posts.
Regarding the sealing of the TOS Bond warehouse, the letter says presenting it as Sheikh Nur Islam’s establishment is “completely false and fabricated.” It claims that neither he nor his family has any direct or indirect connection to it, and that linking them to any incident, activity or allegation involving the company is contrary to the facts.
Describing his businesses, the letter says that in Bangladesh he has no liquor bar, warehouse or diplomatic bonded house other than Fu-Wang Bowling and Services Limited. Apart from that, he has restaurant and agriculture-based businesses in the country.
The letter adds that Sheikh Nur Islam has lived in Canada for 46 years and is a Canadian citizen. His 2 daughters, Disha Islam and Barsha Islam, are Canadian citizens by birth.
It claims he runs and expands his businesses in Bangladesh using remittances sent through proper channels from the income of his legitimate business in Canada.
On Thursday night, a team led by the DNC, together with the Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate and the Special Response Battalion (SRB), raided a bonded warehouse called TOS Bond Private Limited in Gulshan. The warehouse was sealed during the raid.
The DNC announced the raid in a press release the next morning, Friday. The warehouse’s owner is Nur Islam, and the report named him as owner based on information he himself provided.
Sheikh Nur Islam’s side has now denied that ownership information.
The protest letter also mentions the marriage of his daughter Disha Islam to Salman Muqtadir. However, it says he and his family did not accept the marriage and that social and family ties have been cut since then.

item.title: What Bangladesh Bank’s policy rate means for your wallet
item.description:
When Bangladesh Bank announced it was keeping its main interest rate fixed at 9.50%, the economic jargon might have sounded like abstract policy talk.
But behind that single percentage point is a decision that hits close to home—influencing everything from your monthly grocery budget to your chance at a salary raise.
Here is a breakdown of what this policy rate is, why the central bank is holding it high, and how it impacts your daily life.
Think of Bangladesh Bank as the "bank for commercial banks."
When local commercial banks run short on cash, they borrow money from the central bank.
The policy rate (or repo rate) is simply the interest rate Bangladesh Bank charges those commercial banks.
Holding the rate at 9.50% is like putting a firm foot on the economy's brakes to keep inflation from speeding out of control.
While overall price hikes slowed down slightly to 8.26% recently, daily expenses for non-food items—like health, transport, and household items—remain high at 9.32%.
On top of that, global fuel prices and supply chain risks threaten to push costs back up. Keeping the policy rate elevated prevents fresh money from flooding the market and stoking further price spikes.
However, these economic brakes come with a trade-off: business expansion slows down.
With commercial loan rates around 13% to 15%, companies are holding back on building new facilities or upgrading equipment.
Consequently, private sector borrowing has dropped to a low 4.75%, causing overall economic growth to cool down.
How it hits your daily life
For the average household, keeping interest rates high is a mixed bag of daily compromises:
Whether you are applying for a personal loan, a home mortgage, or funding to expand a family business, taking out a loan will cost significantly more in monthly installments. Many families and small business owners are forced to delay major investments until borrowing costs come down.
On the brighter side, high interest rates force banks to offer better returns on deposits. If you or a family member put money into a Fixed Deposit (FDR) or savings account, you will earn higher interest income compared to periods when rates are low.
Because companies find it expensive to borrow capital, they cut back on hiring, freeze salary increments, or postpone growth projects. A fresh university graduate, for example, may find fewer job openings as businesses operate conservatively to manage expenses.
The biggest upside for common households is eventual price stability. When high borrowing costs curb excessive spending across the economy, sellers find it harder to continuously raise prices on daily goods and food items.

Cool down high living costs

item.title: Three motorcyclists killed in Bagerhat road crash, six injured
item.description:
Three motorcyclists were killed and six others were injured in a three-way collision involving two motorcycles and a three-wheeler human hauler (Nosimon) on the Signboard-Bogi regional highway in Morrelganj upazila of Bagerhat on Saturday evening.
The deceased were identified as Limon Molla, 24, son of Babul Molla from the Kalikabari area; Md. Amin Khan, 23, son of Nazrul Islam; and Soheb, 16, son of Jamal Master, both residents of Dona village in the same upazila. Limon and Soheb were students, while Amin Khan was a local grocer, police said.
Md Shahidullah, Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Morrelganj Police Station, said a coconut-laden three-wheeler was heading toward Bagerhat from Morrelganj Ghat when a speeding motorcycle coming from the opposite direction collided head-on with it. Two riders died on the spot, while the third succumbed to his injuries on the way to the health complex.
Moments later, a second motorcycle crashed into the overturned Nosimon and the first motorcycle, injuring six others.
Dr Md Sifat Khan, Acting Morrelganj Upazila Health Officer, said nine people were brought to the health complex following the accident, three of whom were dead on arrival. Among the injured, two were referred to the Khulna Medical College Hospital, while four returned home after receiving primary treatment.
Police seized both motorcycles and the Nosimon, though the driver of the three-wheeler fled the scene. The process of handing over the bodies to their families following legal formalities is underway, OC Shahidullah added.

item.title: Seven detained with gold, phones, laptops at Dhaka airport
item.description:
The Armed Police Battalion (APBn) detained seven people during three separate operations at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Saturday.
The law enforcers also seized around 781.3 grams (about 67 bhori) of gold jewellery, 10 mobile phones, two laptops and three cartons of cigarettes, said Mohammad Nazir Ahmed Khan, Superintendent of Police (Operations) of the Airport (13) Armed Police Battalion,
In the first operation, APBn personnel conducting a covert operation near the northern side of the airport's roundabout noticed a group of people attempting to flee after sensing the presence of law enforcement.
They subsequently detained five people.
After taking them to the Airport APBn office and conducting body searches, officers recovered 484.2 grams of gold jewellery, two laptops, eight mobile phones and three cartons of cigarettes from their possession.
The detainees were identified as Tofazzal Hossain, 37, Jasim Uddin, 39, Arafat Hossain, 28, Arif, 42, and Md Alamin Gazi, 37.
In the second operation, a woman was detained after she was spotted loitering suspiciously on the paved road near Canopy No 2 in the airport's arrival area.
After taking 39-year-old Rupban Begum to the Airport APBn office, officers conducted an interrogation and body search and recovered 98.7 grams of gold jewellery and a mobile phone from her possession.
In the third operation, M A Matin, 30, was detained after he was spotted loitering suspiciously on the paved road west of the roundabout at the airport's main entrance.
A body search following interrogation led to the recovery of 198.4 grams of gold jewellery and a mobile phone from his possession.
During interrogation, the detainees reportedly said the recovered gold jewellery had been brought into Bangladesh from various countries by unidentified passengers for smuggling. The detainees had allegedly been involved with airport-based gold-smuggling syndicates as receivers for a long time.
Three separate cases have been filed against the detainees with Airport Police Station.
Mohammad Nazir Ahmed Khan said Airport APBn continues to play an active role in preventing smuggling and curbing other crimes within the airport area.
“We are firmly committed to preventing all forms of illegal activities, including the smuggling of gold and narcotics. Our operations and intelligence activities to prevent smuggling through the airport will continue,” he said.

What is the most worrying indicator in the economy now?
item.description:
The first three months of the fiscal year, or one quarter, have ended. The government’s revenue collection and spending during this period, the amount it has borrowed from banks, and the extent to which the private sector has received loans all provide an indication of where the economy may be headed.

These figures are not relevant only to economists and policymakers. People’s incomes and livelihoods are directly linked to inflation, employment, business credit, government spending and the foreign-exchange situation.

There is also a legal obligation to conduct quarterly reviews of budget implementation. The Government Finance and Budget Management Act 2009 states that the finance minister must review revenue collection and expenditure trends on a quarterly basis against the budget targets.

A report on the findings of the review and the necessary measures must be presented at the next session of parliament.

During the previous government, however, we saw the assessment of the first three months sometimes being presented in parliament six months later. Towards the end, the regular presentation of such reports also stopped. At least this time, we hope that will not happen.

Even without waiting for the government’s review, however, it is possible to get some idea of the direction of the economy. Much of the economic data is now readily available.

Bangladesh Bank publishes 19 economic indicators every week on its website, in just two pages. If the reports published on 28 June and 27 September this year are placed side by side, they provide a preliminary picture of which indicators improved over the quarter, which deteriorated and where new risks emerged.

There is no scope here to analyse all the indicators. Not all the data have been updated for the full three-month period. Overall, however, it can be said that there is no indicator that is in particularly good shape. Rather, it appears that a further decline has been prevented, but there are no clear signs of recovery.

An analysis of the indicators inevitably raises five questions. Has inflationary pressure really eased? How much has government borrowing increased? Why is private-sector credit growth so low? Is the money supply growing too rapidly? And how sustainable is the improvement in the foreign-exchange and reserve situation?

For today, however, I would like to discuss two of these questions: the growth of government and private-sector borrowing from the banking system. The annual growth in government borrowing stood at 30.37 per cent on 28 June; three months later, it had risen to 34.11 per cent. Over the same period, private-sector credit growth fell further, from 4.75 per cent to 4.62 per cent.

The two figures are deeply concerning. Private-sector credit growth is now at its lowest level in 33 years. This makes an unpleasant picture of the economy clear. Credit growth in the banking system is increasingly being directed towards the government, while private-sector lending remains stagnant.

We know that the government’s revenue is far too low, while expenditure continues to rise. As a result, the government is having to rely increasingly on bank borrowing. At the same time, it is not simply that the private sector is receiving less credit because the government is borrowing more.

In reality, the private sector is not taking loans because of uncertainty surrounding investment. Loans are not cheap either, given the high interest rates. As a result, businesses are not approaching banks unless they really need to.

The energy crisis is one of the major obstacles at present. Some point to high interest rates as well. But historical data from Bangladesh do not support the argument that high interest rates alone are the main reason for the lack of investment.

There is an organisation under the Ministry of Finance called the Institute of Public Finance. In 2025, two joint secretaries of the Ministry of Finance, Abdul Mannan and Asif Iqbal, published a study in its journal.

The central argument of their research is that when the economy performs well and grows, private investment increases subsequently as a result. If businesspeople do not see the potential for markets and the economy to expand, it is difficult to significantly increase investment simply by lowering interest rates or providing incentives.

That is where the problem lies. Our average economic growth has fallen to almost half its previous level. Wages are rising more slowly than inflation. People’s purchasing power has declined. This has reduced overall demand. No one knows when the energy crisis will be resolved. If this is the situation, then who will invest?

For the past four years, the economy’s worst indicator has been high inflation. Setting that aside, the most worrying indicators are perhaps private-sector credit growth and the government’s continued borrowing from banks.

This is because bank credit is increasingly being directed towards government financing rather than the productive private sector. This may allow the government to keep spending for some time, but it will not generate sustainable growth or create employment.

Unless this is addressed quickly, today’s weak credit growth will translate into lower investment, fewer jobs and slower economic growth in the future. Combined with high inflation, that would make for a dangerous picture.

*The author is Prothom Alo’s Head of Online.

* This piece has been translated by Farjana Liakat for Prothom Alo English Online

item.title: 16 govt medical colleges struggle with severe shortages, yet more to come
item.description:
Habiganj 250-bed District Sadar Hospital is located almost at the centre of the city. Habiganj Medical College is housed within this hospital. The government-run college was established in 2016. Even after 10 years, arrangements have not been made for land of its own. The medical college operates from the second, third and eighth floors of the hospital’s eight-storey building.

Habiganj Medical College began its academic activities in 2018 without its own land, buildings or campus. Teaching takes place in five classrooms occupying 3,000 square feet. The college does not have the necessary teachers, practical classrooms or laboratories. Nor does it have accommodation or a hostel for students.

Students at the medical college are disgruntled. One such student, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity said, “Every medical college has its own hospital. Our college does not. We have to depend on the Sadar Hospital. But because the hospital has no registrars, there is no one to supervise our work.”

Prothom Alo’s analysis found that the colleges are operating with significant shortages. Five of the colleges do not have their own land and therefore have no buildings of their own either. All the colleges have teacher shortages with Magura Medical College having 62 per cent of its teaching posts vacant. As accommodation has not been arranged, 67 female students of Patuakhali Medical College are living in an unused building.

It may be noted that registrars provide students with hands-on training in the hospital wards.

This situation is not limited to just one government medical college. There are 110 medical colleges in the country, of which 37 are government-run. Prothom Alo visited 16 government medical colleges facing shortages or crises involving their own land, infrastructure and teachers, and gathered information on their conditions.

These colleges are relatively new, having been established between 2008 and 2020. Prothom Alo reporters visited the medical colleges between August and September.

The colleges include Pabna, Gopalganj, Jashore, Kushtia, Satkhira, Kishoreganj, Tangail, Jamalpur, Patuakhali, Habiganj, Nilphamari, Netrakona, Naogaon, Magura, Chandpur and Sunamganj medical colleges.

All the colleges have teacher shortages with Magura Medical College having 62 per cent of its teaching posts vacant. As accommodation has not been arranged, 67 female students of Patuakhali Medical College are living in an unused building.

Prothom Alo’s investigation found that these medical colleges were established at the behest of individuals. Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister who was ousted from power in the July mass uprising, had said that a medical college would be established in every district.

The establishment of medical colleges did not stop after her ouster. The interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus also approved medical colleges without resolving all the various existing problems. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government is following the same path.

Netrokona Medical College was established in 2018 at the initiative of Sazzadul Hasan, then secretary at the Prime Minister’s Office, and with the support of the Ministry of Health. Yet the government-run college does not have any land of its own. The college received administrative and academic approval without decisions being made on where its hospital would be located in Netrokona or how land would be acquired.

College in someone else’s premises

Private medical colleges have to be established in accordance with laws and regulations. They are required to have their own land, their own buildings and their own hospitals. But there are no laws or regulations governing the establishment of government medical colleges.

Medical colleges are being established one after another at the initiative of influential individuals and with the support of the Ministry of Health. Medical colleges are not being established based on assessments of whether there is an actual need for them.

According to sources at the Directorate General of Medical Education (DGME), Netrokona Medical College was established in 2018 at the initiative of Sazzadul Hasan, then secretary at the Prime Minister’s Office, and with the support of the Ministry of Health. Yet the government-run college does not have any land of its own.

The college received administrative and academic approval without decisions being made on where its hospital would be located in Netrokona or how land would be acquired. Eight years after its establishment, the college still has no building of its own, no hospital and no campus. Yet many students have graduated from the college with MBBS degrees and are now practising as physicians.

On 31 August, several students of Pabna Medical College told Prothom Alo that although the college was established in 2008, it still does not have its own hospital. The district Sadar Hospital is about eight kilometres from the college. Students have to travel there by bus every day. The road is full of potholes. There is only one bus for 240 students. Travelling to and from the hospital is a painful experience.

The medical college is using four buildings built to accommodate physicians on the northern side of Netrokona 250-bed Sadar Hospital as its academic buildings. In reality, the medical college is operating in someone else’s premises. Students are dissatisfied with the situation. They have even held human chains demanding a permanent campus.

Apart from Habiganj and Netrokona, three other medical colleges have no land at all. They are Naogaon, Magura and Nilphamari medical colleges. Classes at these colleges are held at the respective district sadar hospitals. The process of purchasing land for Chandpur Medical College is under way. The college is operating from several rooms at the district Sadar Hospital.

Six medical colleges grapple with lack of infrastructure, teacher, learning facilities

The remaining 10 colleges have land and their own college buildings. These are Pabna, Gopalganj, Jashore, Kushtia, Satkhira, Kishoreganj, Tangail, Jamalpur, Patuakhali and Sunamganj medical colleges. However, Pabna, Jashore and Jamalpur medical colleges still do not have their own hospitals.

On 31 August, several students of Pabna Medical College told Prothom Alo that although the college was established in 2008, it still does not have its own hospital. The district Sadar Hospital is about eight kilometres from the college. Students have to travel there by bus every day. The road is full of potholes. There is only one bus for 240 students. Travelling to and from the hospital is a painful experience.

It was found that all 16 medical colleges are facing teacher shortages. The situation is most acute at Magura Medical College. The college has 84 teaching posts, but only 32 teachers are working there. Fifty-two teaching posts are vacant. In other words, the college is providing education with 62 per cent of its teaching posts unfilled.

No teachers

Classroom-based teaching and learning, as well as hands-on learning and training, are equally important at medical colleges. Both require an adequate number of teachers. Medical students have to sit for various examinations, both major and minor, on a regular basis. This also requires close supervision by teachers.

When there are too few teachers, students fall short in both their understanding and hands-on learning. Proper supervision also becomes impossible.

It was found that all 16 medical colleges are facing teacher shortages. The situation is most acute at Magura Medical College. The college has 84 teaching posts, but only 32 teachers are working there. Fifty-two teaching posts are vacant. In other words, the college is providing education with 62 per cent of its teaching posts unfilled.

The Directorate General of Medical Education and the Ministry of Health are not overseeing who is teaching in the classrooms, how courses are being completed, who is providing hands-on training or who is conducting examinations.

At Sunamganj Medical College, there are 94 teaching posts, of which only 52 are filled. Forty-five per cent of the posts are vacant. Satkhira Medical College has 103 teaching posts, with 39 per cent vacant. There is no scope to say that the situation is satisfactory at the remaining 13 medical colleges either.

Two female students of Pabna Medical College told Prothom Alo that before enrolling, they had no idea that government medical colleges faced so many problems. There are not even enough teachers to conduct classes. They said their ‘item’ and ‘card’ examinations are completed in a perfunctory manner.

An examination conducted after teaching a small topic, such as a finger or the palm of the hand, is known as an ‘item’ examination. After students are taught many such small topics and after siting for a number of item examinations, they take a ‘card’ examination covering the subject as a whole, such as the entire hand. In medical education, item and card examinations continue throughout the year.

A researcher working at an international research institution, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said that in reality, item and card examinations are not being conducted properly. “The state has not ensured that students go through this process. This is negligence on the part of the state,” the researcher said.

42pc posts of teachers vacant in medical colleges

Shortage of teachers in basic subjects

Eight subjects are considered basic in medical education: anatomy, biochemistry, community medicine, forensic medicine, microbiology, pathology, pharmacology and physiology. These 16 medical colleges are facing a severe shortage of teachers in all eight subjects.

According to information obtained from the DGME, there are 272 posts for professors, associate professors and assistant professors in these 16 medical colleges. Only 100 are currently filled. In other words, 172 posts, or 63 per cent, are vacant in the basic subjects.

After the Awami League government was ousted amid the mass uprising on 5 August 2024, an interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus took charge. Reforming various sectors, or taking initiatives to reform them, was the main task of that government. However, like many other sectors, the interim government could not carry out any reforms in medical education either.

The situation is worst at Naogaon Medical College Hospital. There are 14 posts for professors, associate professors and assistant professors in the basic subjects at the college, and all of them are vacant.

The situation is the next worst at Magura Medical College, where 13 of the 14 posts are vacant. At Sunamganj Medical College, 12 of 14 posts are vacant, while at Habiganj Medical College, 11 of 14 posts are vacant. Pabna Medical College, established in 2008 is still facing a shortage of teachers in the basic subjects, with 50 per cent of the posts for teachers in these subjects vacant.

Professor Md Ruhul Quddus, principal of Pabna Medical College, told Prothom Alo that although the college is 18 years old, it still has a shortage of teachers in the eight basic subjects. There has been only one teacher in biochemistry since 2016, and he is the teacher himself. There are no teachers in gynaecology at all.

In medical colleges where there is not even a single teacher in any of the eight subjects, or where seven of the subjects have no teacher at all, who teaches the students? How are tutorials and examinations conducted in these subjects?

In response to these questions, DGME Director General Professor Nazmul Hossain told Prothom Alo that this was a serious problem, but efforts were being made to overcome it.

Some measures have been taken, such as appointing retired teachers on a contractual basis, increasing incentives to 100 per cent of their salaries, and providing a monthly stipend of Tk 20,000 to students who want to study the basic subjects, he said.

In addition, actively considering having the same teacher teach at multiple medical colleges and conducting classes online in these subjects is also under consideration, added the DGME director general.

Although work to establish Narsingdi Medical College began during the interim government’s tenure, the college received administrative approval from the ministry after the BNP government took office. However, land for the college has yet to be finalised. For now, work of Narsingdi Medical College is expected to begin at the 100-bed Narsingdi District Hospital, according to ministry sources.

Interim government’s inaction

After the Awami League government was ousted amid the mass uprising on 5 August 2024, an interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus took charge. Reforming various sectors, or taking initiatives to reform them, was the main task of that government. However, like many other sectors, the interim government could not carry out any reforms in medical education either.

The interim government did not arrange land for medical colleges that had no land of their own and were operating on others’ premises. It did not take initiatives to appoint teachers to colleges facing severe teacher shortages; instead, it was in the process of approving new government medical colleges.

During the interim government’s tenure, a government medical college was approved in Munshiganj, the district of Home Affairs and Agriculture Adviser Jahangir Alam Chowdhury. Documents show that Public Works Adviser Adilur Rahman Khan had recommended the establishment of this medical college. However, the initiative to establish the college has now come to a complete halt.

During the interim government’s tenure, approval was also given for the Bangladesh Navy to establish a medical college. The college is located in the hospital gate area on the airport road in Chattogram.

Besides, initial work began on establishing a medical college in Narsingdi. Officials from the Ministry of Health and the Directorate General of Health Services had visited the area and gave opinion in favour of establishing the medical college.

Regardless of whether land, a hospital or teachers are available, the BNP government wants to establish more government medical colleges. According to Health Ministry sources, the process of establishing two medical colleges in Bhola and Joypurhat has begun. Ministry officials have already visited the two districts.

BNP following the same path

Although work to establish Narsingdi Medical College began during the interim government’s tenure, the college received administrative approval from the ministry after the BNP government took office. However, land for the college has yet to be finalised. For now, work of Narsingdi Medical College is expected to begin at the 100-bed Narsingdi District Hospital, according to ministry sources.

Generally, a hospital with at least 250 beds is required to establish a medical college. However, Narsingdi has no such hospital. Even the existing 100-bed hospital does not have adequate staff. Work is underway to upgrade the hospital to 250 beds.

Soon after the BNP government was formed, Thakurgaon Medical College was approved. The development project proposal (DPP) for the college is nearing finalisation. The college will be located beside the Thakurgaon-Dinajpur highway, about five kilometres from Thakurgaon town. There is an initiative to enrol students at Thakurgaon and Narsingdi medical colleges in the 2026–27 academic year.

Regardless of whether land, a hospital or teachers are available, the BNP government wants to establish more government medical colleges. According to Health Ministry sources, the process of establishing two medical colleges in Bhola and Joypurhat has begun. Ministry officials have already visited the two districts.

DGME Director General Professor Nazmul Hossain told Prothom Alo, “We have received applications from a total of 12 districts.”

Referring to the formation of a seven-member committee headed by the state minister of health to assess proposals for establishing new medical colleges, he said, “With the support of the World Health Organization, work is underway to assess the demand or need for workforce in 25 areas of medical education up to 2041.”

“The report will be available by October. Based on the report, the seven-member committee will then decide on the medical colleges. However, after Thakurgaon and Narsingdi, the government is not approving any new government medical colleges for the time being,” he added.

Even after many years since their establishment, many have failed to become full-fledged medical colleges. These colleges cannot provide medical education while maintaining proper standards, nor can they produce quality physicians.

Is it possible to produce quality physicians?

The country’s first medical college, Dhaka Medical College, was established in 1946. Before independence, there were seven medical colleges, all of them government-run. Since independence, another 103 government and private medical colleges have been established.

Of the 110 medical colleges, 37 are government-run and seven are under the armed forces—one Armed Forces Medical College, five Army Medical Colleges and one Navy Medical College. There are also 66 private medical colleges.

Most of these 110 medical colleges face infrastructure crisis, a lack of the required number of teachers and shortages of educational materials. Experts believe that many medical colleges should not even have remained operational if there were no compromise with irregularities and corruption.

Abu Jamil Faisel graduated with an MBBS degree from Mymensingh Medical College in 1976. After graduating, he joined government service. He later left government service to work in the private sector and was involved in research for a long time. This public health expert told Prothom Alo that most medical colleges were established for political reasons.

Even after many years since their establishment, many have failed to become full-fledged medical colleges. These colleges cannot provide medical education while maintaining proper standards, nor can they produce quality physicians. It is true that there is deep public discontent over the standard of healthcare in the country. These colleges are behind this discontent, he said.

[The report was prepared with information provided by staff correspondents in Kushtia, Tangail, Habiganj and Sunamganj; the Jashore office; and correspondents in Satkhira, Gopalganj, Kishoreganj, Patuakhali, Jamalpur, Chandpur, Netrakona, Magura, Nilphamari, Pabna and Naogaon.]

item.title: Akhtaruzzaman warned people to beware of Jamaat, later joined the party himself
item.description:
About six months before the 12th parliamentary election held on 7 January 2024, Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman met then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who has since been ousted from power.

At the time, he had been expelled from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) for the fifth time. He nevertheless contested the election as an independent candidate from the Kishoreganj-2 constituency.

During his campaign, Akhtaruzzaman said, “Even if I sleep at home, I will win. That is the political reality.” He ultimately lost his deposit in the election. The election, widely described as a “dummy” election, was boycotted by the BNP and other opposition parties at the time.

Before the 2024 election, in an interview with local journalists in Kishoreganj, Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman described Jamaat-e-Islami as a “party that cuts tendons” and warned party activists to be cautious about the organisation.

At various times, he has also described Jamaat as “Razakars” and “war criminals” over its controversial role in 1971. Yet, before the 13th parliamentary election, he joined Jamaat on 13 December. He did not contest the election.

During the July mass uprising of 2024, Akhtaruzzaman appeared on a social-media-based talk show on 15 July and said, “All the Razakars, war criminals and Jamaat are involved in this [the movement].”

He also called all the protesters “children of Razakars” and said in an agitated tone, “They are against the Liberation War. One hundred times. I am saying this categorically. Look at their family backgrounds.”

Yet in the post-uprising political landscape, he joined Jamaat, which has been vocal about the July uprising in its rallies, speeches and statements.

Such contradictions have made Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman a frequently discussed figure throughout his political career.

He was arrested on Friday in a case over creating disorder at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka amid a shortage of luggage trolleys, obstructing government duties and physically assaulting a security official on duty. A Dhaka court granted him one day’s remand on Saturday.

During the incident on 1 October, he also publicly threatened the airport’s executive director, Group Captain SM Ragib Samad, saying, “I’ll beat you up and drag you out” and “I’ll drag you out by the neck.” After a video of the incident spread on social media, criticism intensified. He was subsequently arrested.

A 71-member delegation comprising Jamaat lawmakers, their family members and party leaders had visited several countries. Akhtaruzzaman was also part of the delegation. The incident occurred on the day of their return.

There have, however, been various complaints about mismanagement at Shahjalal International Airport. Following the incident, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat visited the airport on Friday night, spoke to passengers and instructed officials to improve services.

Threats to tear out tongues, controversial remarks about enforced disappearances

Akhtaruzzaman has attracted attention for his remarks since the beginning of his political career. He has been a regular participant in various television and social-media-based talk shows. At times, he has been seen behaving aggressively towards fellow panellists during heated discussions.

Before the 13th parliamentary election, Akhtaruzzaman got into an argument with senior journalist Mahbub Kamal during a talk show. Angry with Mahbub Kamal, he said, “Why are you speaking so rudely? Why are you challenging me? Don’t do this.” Mahbub Kamal apologised, but Akhtaruzzaman did not stop.

In another talk show in March, Akhtaruzzaman became involved in a heated debate with Tarek Rahman, member secretary of the Amjanatar Dal. During the argument, Akhtaruzzaman told him, “Your tongue needs to be torn out.”

At one point, he said, “The practice of enforced disappearances and killings comes for politicians like Tarek Rahman.” Referring to Tarek’s past experience of being a victim of enforced disappearance, he also told him, “If someone like you is not going to disappear, then who will?”

Earlier this year, Akhtaruzzaman got into an argument with Joban magazine editor Rezaul Karim Rony over Jamaat’s historical responsibilities, including its role in 1971.

Akhtaruzzaman said, “Jamaat was on Pakistan’s side until 16 December, but they did not commit genocide.” Rony, himself a freedom fighter, urged him not to make such a claim and said Jamaat had participated in the genocide. Akhtaruzzaman replied, “I will say it a hundred times, a thousand times. There is evidence.”

Meeting with Sheikh Hasina

Akhtaruzzaman contested the 2018 11th parliamentary election from Kishoreganj-2 on a BNP ticket but lost. Although he was expelled from the party for the fifth time in 2022, he continued to appear regularly on various talk shows.

About six months before the 12th parliamentary election, on 8 June 2023, Akhtaruzzaman visited Ganabhaban and met then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina. On behalf of “Kishoreganj Green Power”, he handed Sheikh Hasina a written application seeking permission to establish a 70MW solar power plant. The initiative was being led by his son, Sabbir Zaman.

After that meeting, Akhtaruzzaman became highly complimentary of Sheikh Hasina in various statements. At the same time, he strongly criticised Tarique Rahman, then acting chairman of the BNP and now its chairman and prime minister, during various talk shows.

In one talk show at the time, he said, “Our leader, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, is like the ten-armed goddess. She is handling everything on her own.”

Expelled from the BNP five times

Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman was born in 1951 in Katiadi upazila of Kishoreganj. His nickname is Ranjan. He was serving in the Bangladesh Army during the 7 November 1975 Sipahi–Janata Revolution. Akhtaruzzaman joined the BNP when the party was founded.

He was elected to parliament twice in a row, in 1991 and 1996, from Kishoreganj-2 on a BNP ticket. At the time, the constituency comprised only Katiadi upazila. Pakundia upazila was later added to the constituency. He also served at one point as president of the Kishoreganj district BNP.

He has frequently remained in the spotlight over various statements criticising the party and its leaders, and the BNP has taken organisational action against him.

Akhtaruzzaman was first expelled from the BNP in 1996. At the time, the opposition Awami League was leading a movement demanding the introduction of a caretaker government system.

The BNP, then in government, initially refused to accept the demand. Akhtaruzzaman told the media that the demand for a caretaker government came from the people and that the BNP should accept it. Following those remarks, he was expelled from the BNP for the first time.

In 2000, the then-opposition BNP decided to boycott a session of parliament. Akhtaruzzaman defied the party decision and attended the session. As a result, his parliamentary seat became vacant under Article 70 of the Constitution.

Although he challenged the decision in court, the seat remained vacant until the dissolution of the seventh parliament in July 2001. He was expelled from the BNP for the second time over the incident.

In 2014, Major Akhtaruzzaman was expelled from the party for the third time after making indecent remarks about current BNP Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. He was expelled for the fourth time after criticising senior BNP leaders. On each of those four occasions, however, his expulsion was later revoked.

Most recently, in February 2022, Akhtaruzzaman appeared on a private television talk show and said, “The BNP has no shame, no vision. Their leaders will feel ashamed when the activists beat them with shoes.” He was expelled from the party for the fifth time on 20 February that year. He has not returned to the party since.

Before the 13th parliamentary election, however, he formally announced in November that he would work in support of the BNP-nominated candidate in Kishoreganj-2. This once again sparked speculation that he might return to the BNP.

Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman arrested in case over airport disorder and assault on official

Finally, Jamaat

After his final expulsion, Akhtaruzzaman did not join any political party for nearly four years. He remained active, however, through television talk shows and other platforms.

On 13 December, before the last parliamentary election, Akhtaruzzaman visited Jamaat’s central office in Moghbazar, Dhaka, met the party’s ameer Shafiqur Rahman, the current opposition leader in parliament, and formally joined the organisation by filling out a preliminary associate membership form.

The move generated considerable discussion at the time because Akhtaruzzaman had a long history of opposition to Jamaat. In 1991, when the BNP formed the government with Jamaat’s support, he was among those who opposed the arrangement.

Most recently, in an interview as an independent candidate during the 2024 parliamentary election, Akhtaruzzaman said, “It doesn’t matter if Jamaat-e-Islami is a terrorist organisation. They are a party that cuts tendons. I would urge BNP leaders and activists, particularly those in Katiadi and Pakundia, to be cautious. Beware of Jamaat, and beware of those within my party who are secretly aligned with Jamaat.”

Regarding the controversial election, he said, “This election is going well, it is fair, and efforts are being made to make it free. The Election Commission is doing a good job. However, Jamaat-e-Islami is trying to boycott and obstruct the election and is placing the responsibility for this on the BNP.”

After joining Jamaat in December, however, Akhtaruzzaman told this correspondent on 18 December that he had joined the organisation consciously and after observing its activities closely. “There have been many changes in Jamaat’s activities and statements,” he said.

Former student coordinator Abdul Kader, who came into prominence during the July uprising after announcing a nine-point demand, has questioned whether Jamaat provided Akhtaruzzaman with “shelter” after the uprising.

On Saturday afternoon, Kader wrote on Facebook, “Why was Akhtaruzzaman not brought to justice after the uprising? Yet this man went to the media and opposed the movement, legitimised the government’s attacks and cases against students by labelling them in various ways, openly defended the killer Hasina, and even took to the streets against students during July!”

item.title: Former donor member locks school over “failure to give daughter-in-law job”
item.description:
A former donor member of the management committee of a school in Puthia, Rajshahi, has planted banana trees on the school field and locked the teachers’ office.

He also fenced off the school’s main entrance with bamboo. He said he took these steps because the school did not give his daughter-in-law a job and changed its name. However, the headteacher said the school had given his daughter-in-law a job.

The school is named Bhalukgachi Muktijoddha School. When it was established in 2015, it was called Muktijoddha Technical School and College.

On Saturday, the weekly holiday, former donor member of the management committee Azad Ali brought several people to the school, planted banana trees on the field and put another padlock on the lock attached to the teachers’ office.

According to school sources, when the school was established, the plan was to teach students from pre-primary to secondary and higher secondary levels.

However, the institution did not have permission to provide higher secondary education. It only offered primary education. Following the political changeover on 5 August, the Rajshahi Education Board sent a letter seeking a change to the institution’s name.

The school management committee then held a meeting and named it “Bhalukgachi Muktijoddha School”. The resolution states that Azad Ali, who was then a donor member, himself proposed the name.

On 11 December 2024, the institution received permission to provide lower secondary education up to class eight. However, it has not been brought under the MPO scheme.

Students currently study at the primary level and in classes six and seven. As students progress to higher classes, the institution will have to obtain approval for secondary and higher secondary education.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, Azad Ali brought several people to the school and put another lock on the lock attached to the teachers’ office. He also fenced off the main entrance with bamboo and planted banana trees on the field.

Local shopkeeper Lal Mohammad told Prothom Alo, “There used to be many students at the school. Their number has fallen because of the lawsuit. Classes are still held, though. Today, Azad Ali suddenly came and fenced off the school in this way. As a result, we cannot even collect water from the school’s tube well.”

When asked about the matter, Azad Ali told Prothom Alo that he had been a donor member of the institution.

He said, “They promised to establish a technical college there and give jobs to my son and daughter-in-law. But they did not establish any institution like a technical college. They did not give my daughter-in-law a job either. That is why I locked the school and planted banana trees.”

Headteacher Selim Reza said, “Azad Ali donated the land to the institution unconditionally. He gave an undertaking on a Tk 300 stamp paper and asked us to start the institution’s activities. After constructing the buildings, when he went to register the land in the institution’s name, he demanded jobs for his son in the vocational section and his daughter-in-law in the college section. The committee had no choice but to agree and registered the land.”

The headteacher further said, “As it took time to formally launch the college section, Azad Ali arranged for his daughter-in-law to join the primary section as an assistant teacher. She died in 2022 while still employed. He then arranged a second marriage for his son and asked the committee to give his son’s new wife a job as a clerk in the secondary section. The committee agreed to that as well.

There is a proper resolution on this matter too. About a year later, on 16 September 2025, he filed a case at a court in Rajshahi. He claimed that the institution had not been established under the name for which he had donated the land. The case is still pending. In this situation, he has locked the institution and planted banana trees on the field.”

Mohammad Touhidul Islam, president of the school’s managing committee and general secretary of Bhalukgachi Union BNP, told Prothom Alo, “An institution does not become established in a day. The donor member’s claim is not correct. The institution has students and classes are being held regularly. The Rajshahi Education Board approved the new managing committee on the 10th of last month.”

When contacted, Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Liaquat Salman told Prothom Alo that he was aware of the matter.

He said he was in Dhaka and would return on Sunday and take steps to reopen the institution. “Whatever may have happened in the past, no one can shut down an institution if it has students,” he said.
